sources.title: Mendel's own 1866 paper, Versuche über Pflanzen-Hybriden ("Experiments on Plant Hybridization")

Historical accounts of Mendel's roughly eight years of pea-plant breeding experiments at the Augustinian monastery of St. Thomas in Brno, and the near-total lack of scientific recognition of his work during his lifetime

analytical_rigor.rationale: Designed and executed a controlled breeding experiment across roughly 28,000 pea plants over eight years, tracking seven distinct heritable traits and applying statistical/mathematical analysis to the resulting ratios to infer discrete units of heredity, documented directly via his own 1866 paper's detailed methodology and data.

detail_orientation.rationale: Systematically tracked and quantified the inheritance patterns of seven distinct pea-plant traits across multiple generations of tens of thousands of individual plants, documented directly via the granular numerical data presented in his own surviving paper.

persistence.rationale: Sustained the pea-plant breeding experiments across roughly eight years of careful, repetitive controlled crossing and counting, documented via his own paper's account of the experiment's duration and the sheer scale of the tracked plant population.

independent_thinking.rationale: Proposed discrete, particulate units of heredity following statistically predictable ratios, departing sharply from the prevailing blending-inheritance assumptions of his era, inferred as genuinely independent scientific judgment from the documented novelty of this conceptual framework relative to contemporary biological thought.

curiosity.rationale: Also conducted meteorological observations and beekeeping experiments alongside his primary plant-hybridization work at the monastery, inferred as some real intellectual range beyond his single best-known project from this documented secondary activity.

mastery_orientation.rationale: Refined his experimental method across the multi-year pea-plant study, moving from initial trait selection to increasingly systematic quantitative tracking, inferred as sustained methodological development from the documented structure of the study as described in his own paper.
